answers.q: Where do I start?
answers.a: Start with part 1, Start here. Read the basics page to get the words straight, then set up your machine in module 00. That takes about a week, before week 1. Then open module 01 and connect your GitHub journal on the Practice page.

answers.q: What are the four parts of the program?
answers.a: 1 Start here: the basics and setting up your machine. 2 Modules: eleven modules from the FDE role to the final project. 3 Practice: one real project worked through 13 steps, with evidence saved to your GitHub journal. 4 Crash course: checked videos, articles and courses to go deeper whenever you need.

answers.q: How long does the program take?
answers.a: The program runs for 12 weeks at about 24 to 32 hours a week. Start here takes about a week before week 1. Modules 01 to 10 run through weeks 1 to 10, and the final project runs in weeks 11 and 12.

answers.q: Which track am I on, and why do we work in pairs?
answers.a: Track A is for people with a software or digital background; the program adds business analysis, discovery and communication. Track B is for domain people such as quality, supply chain or clinical; the program adds code, APIs, data and deployment. Learners work in mixed pairs, one from each track, so they teach each other. After a skills check, Track A can fast-track module 3 and Track B can fast-track module 4.

answers.q: How is my progress checked?
answers.a: There are three layers. Every step of the learning path saves evidence to your GitHub journal and must pass defined checks. A mentor runs checkpoints in weeks 2, 4, 6, 10 and 12. At the end a panel scores you on the rubric.

answers.q: What are the mentor checkpoints?
answers.a: Week 2: a knowledge check on LLM concepts and a prompt log review. Week 4: a skills check, a small coding task for the domain track or an industry brief for the software track. Week 6: a recorded discovery role-play with a mock client. Week 10: a POC demo with evaluation results. Week 12: the final review panel.

answers.q: How do I graduate, and what is the rubric?
answers.a: The panel scores seven dimensions as not yet, practitioner or FDE-ready: discovery, problem framing and value, solution options, build quality, evaluation and safety, deployment and operations, and communication. To graduate you need FDE-ready in discovery, build quality, evaluation and safety, and communication, and at least practitioner in the rest. There is no score for how advanced the technology is.

answers.q: What is the learning path on the Practice page?
keywords: what do i do on practice
answers.a: It is your own path through the program. You connect a GitHub journal, choose a domain and one real project, answer six questions on how to build it, then work through 13 steps over 12 weeks: A basics, B setup, then 01 to 11, one per module. Each step has resources, a task and a done-when line, and saves evidence to your repository.

answers.q: Why do I need a GitHub journal?
answers.a: Your journal is where your evidence lives, so anyone you share it with can see exactly what you have done. Your mentor or manager opens one link to see progress. Over the weeks it becomes a dated record of real work, labs and fixes that you can show in interviews.

answers.q: How do I connect my journal repository?
answers.a: On the Practice page, sign in with GitHub and enter a repository name; fde-learning-journal is suggested. If it does not exist, the page creates it. The page asks for permission to write to your public repositories so it can save your evidence there. The access key stays in that browser tab.

answers.q: When does a step count as done?
keywords: why is my step not done
answers.a: A step is done only when its evidence file is saved in your journal and passes the checks. The checks look for every required field, links that start with https://, a minimum number of words, numbers where they are needed, and no placeholder words such as todo or tbd. The tracker counts what you save and commit, not how good the work is; your mentor's review is what counts.

answers.q: How are points calculated?
answers.a: Each step is worth up to 20 points. You get 10 when your evidence passes the checks, 5 when the time is met, and 5 for at least one commit under projects/ during the step. If you save before the time is met and confirm you went through everything, the time part gives 2 instead of 5. Steps without timed resources get the 5 time points.

answers.q: What does time met mean?
answers.a: The clock starts when you first open a step's resources. Time is met when the stated minutes of those resources plus 30 percent have passed since then. If you save earlier, the page asks you to confirm you went through all the resources, and your answer is saved with the step.

answers.q: What is fde.py and what are its commands?
answers.a: fde.py is a small helper in your journal that uses the same files as the Practice page, so you can track progress from your own machine. Run it from your journal folder: init creates projects/<your-project>/, status shows every step, next says what to do, open STEP opens the resources and starts the clock, log STEP writes and checks your evidence then commits and pushes, check STEP runs the checks without saving, and sync pulls the latest. It needs Python 3.9 or newer; on Windows use py fde.py.

answers.q: Can I edit the files in the fde folder by hand?
answers.a: Please do not. The tools read the data line at the end of each file, and changing it can break your progress. Use the Practice page or fde.py for those files. Put your own notes, code and drafts anywhere else, for example notes/, labs/ or drafts/.

answers.q: How does the module test work?
answers.a: Each module test has 20 questions from that module. The pass mark is 80 percent, which is 16 of 20. You have up to 3 attempts, with 24 hours between attempts. After a failed attempt the result lists the lessons to review.

answers.q: What happens if I fail the module test three times?
answers.a: After 3 failed attempts a mentor goes through the module with you and then resets your attempts in your journal. Until then, review the lessons, especially the ones listed in your last result.

answers.q: What is the crash course?
answers.a: The crash course is a library of 431 checked videos, articles, courses, books and papers in seven areas: systems and networking, programming, databases and data, cloud and DevOps, security and privacy, AI and LLMs, and the FDE role and business skills. In each area do the Must do items first; they are short and cover each topic once. Come back to Recommended and Go deeper when a lesson or project needs more.

answers.q: Which certifications should I get?
answers.a: Certificates are optional and never replace the final project. Start with the Anthropic Academy ones (Claude API, Claude Code and MCP courses), then one paid exam that matches your clients' cloud or your gap, such as AWS Certified AI Practitioner, Azure AI Fundamentals, Google Cloud Generative AI Leader, IIBA ECBA or a GitHub certification. Step 02 asks for the AI Fluency certificate.

answers.q: How does this help chat work?
answers.a: It answers from the course's prepared answers first. If none fits and you have connected Cloudflare on the Practice page, it asks your own Cloudflare Workers AI, using the page you are on as context. AI answers can be wrong, so check them against the lessons.

answers.q: What is the tutor on the Practice page?
answers.a: When you press Ask the tutor, the checks give the verdict first. Then an AI model run by the program reads your idea or evidence and suggests up to three improvements. The suggestions can be wrong, and the checks, not the tutor, decide when a step is done.

answers.q: How do I choose my practice project?
answers.a: Pick a project from the industry you know or want to work in, then answer six questions on how to build it. The guide recommends a setup and you write why it fits; this goes into your project file. Use synthetic or public data only, never real client or personal data.

answers.q: What is an LLM?
answers.a: A large language model is a language model with billions of parameters, trained on a very large amount of text and code to predict the next piece of text. Examples are Claude, GPT, Gemini and Llama. The same model can sort tickets, draft emails, read contracts and write SQL. It computes a likely answer from learned patterns; it does not look answers up.

answers.q: What is a token?
answers.a: A token is the unit an LLM reads and writes: a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. A common rule of thumb for English is that 100 tokens is about 75 words. Prices, limits and speed are all measured in tokens.

answers.q: What is context and the context window?
answers.a: Context is everything the model can see for one request: the system prompt, conversation history, documents, tool results and your latest message. The context window is the maximum amount of that, in tokens, including the answer. If a fact is not in its training and not in the context, the model can only guess. Every token costs money and time, so send what matters.

answers.q: What is a harness?
answers.a: A harness is the software around a model that turns it into a working tool. It builds the prompt, keeps the conversation, offers tools, runs them when the model asks, and decides when to stop. The model is the engine; the harness is the rest of the car. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and your own agent code are all harnesses.

answers.q: What is an agent?
answers.a: An agent is a model working in a loop: plan, use a tool, look at the result, continue, until the task is done. It is powerful but harder to predict and test. Use a simple fixed workflow when that is enough.

answers.q: What is RAG?
answers.a: RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, first searches your documents for the passages that matter, then puts them into the context with the question and asks the model to answer from them. It is the standard way to answer from client documents with citations, without retraining anything.

answers.q: What is MCP?
answers.a: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A system is exposed once as an MCP server, and any app that supports MCP can use it. Think of it as a USB-C port for AI tools. It lets a client connect their systems once and reuse them across AI tools.

answers.q: What is the difference between open-weight and closed models?
answers.a: A closed model, such as Claude or Gemini, has unpublished weights and you use it through the provider's app, API or a cloud partner. An open-weight model, such as Llama or Gemma, has published weights you can download and run under its license. Open-weight can run inside a client's network, but then you own hosting, scaling, updates and safety testing. Many models called open are open-weight only, not fully open source.

answers.q: What is the difference between the Claude app and the API?
answers.a: The Claude app is a product for people chatting. The Anthropic API is a service for programs, paid per token with an API key from the Claude Console. Same models, but different billing, different controls and often different data terms. A chat app is great for research and drafting; an automated process uses the API.

answers.q: What is a VPC?
answers.a: A Virtual Private Cloud is your own isolated private network inside a public cloud. You decide its addresses and what can reach the internet. Think of a locked private office floor in a shared tower. Client data usually lives inside a VPC, so your POC may need to run in it or connect to it securely.

answers.q: What is PII?
answers.a: PII is personal data: information that identifies a person directly or indirectly, such as name, email, phone number and ID numbers, and under many laws also location and online identifiers. Most privacy laws attach duties to it, so spot it before it goes anywhere. Use only the data the task needs and mask the rest.

answers.q: What is the difference between privacy and security?
answers.a: Privacy is about the rules for using personal data: are we allowed to use this data in this way? Security is about protecting data: can anyone who should not see it get to it? You can be perfectly secure and still break privacy rules, for example by using data for a purpose people never agreed to.

answers.q: What is prompt injection?
answers.a: Prompt injection is an attack where text inside a document, email or web page contains instructions meant to make the model do something else, such as reveal data or call a tool. Any content the model reads can try to steer it. Limit what tools and data it can reach, and keep a person in the loop for risky actions.

answers.q: What is a hallucination?
answers.a: A hallucination is when a model states something false with confidence, such as an invented citation or a policy clause that does not exist. It follows from predicting likely text without checking facts. Ground answers in sources and measure them on real cases.

answers.q: What are embeddings?
answers.a: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. An embedding model makes them. They let you search documents by meaning, not just keywords, which is the search step inside most RAG systems.

answers.q: What do I need to set up before module 1?
answers.a: Seven things: a GitHub account, Git, the VS Code editor, Python 3 plus Node.js, at least one AI coding assistant, a chat app for thinking, and a learning journal repository. Module 00 walks through each install in order. If you have never used a terminal, that is fine.

answers.q: Which AI coding assistant should I start with?
answers.a: You only need one to start. Copilot inside VS Code is the gentlest start because it needs no terminal install. Add Claude Code or Codex later if you or your employer already pay for a plan. Plans change often, so check the official pricing page before you pay.

answers.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub, and commit and push?
answers.a: Git is a program on your computer that tracks changes in a folder. GitHub is a website that hosts repositories. Commit is saving a snapshot on your machine; push is backing it up to GitHub. You can commit ten times offline and push once.

answers.q: Why should I turn on two-factor authentication?
answers.a: A client's IT team will ask whether two-factor is on before they give you access, and this account becomes your portfolio. With 2FA, signing in needs your password plus a second proof. Save the recovery codes somewhere safe, such as a password manager, or losing your phone can lock you out.

answers.q: What is a virtual environment and why do I need one?
answers.a: A virtual environment is a private box of Python packages for one project, so upgrading a package for one project cannot break another. Create one per project with python3 -m venv .venv, then activate it. Add .venv to your .gitignore so it is never committed.

answers.q: How do I stay in control of what the AI assistant runs?
answers.a: Coding assistants can read files, edit them and run commands, and each tool asks for approval depending on its settings. While learning, let it ask before every file edit and command, and read each request. If you would not run a command yourself, say no and ask why. Open only your learning folder, never your whole home folder.

answers.q: What goes in my learning journal?
answers.a: Each day you study, add a short entry: what you learned, what you built, what broke and how you fixed it, open questions and links. Commit and push at least once per day you study, and once a week record a 2 to 5 minute video explaining one lab. What broke and how you fixed it is the most valuable part. Never put employer or client information in it.

answers.q: What is a forward deployed engineer?
answers.a: An FDE is an engineer who works with one client, close to the people who do the work, and builds a solution for their real problem. A general model does not know a client's data, rules, systems or habits, and the FDE closes that gap. You find how the work really happens, build a proof of concept, measure it and help the client run it after you leave.

answers.q: What are the steps of the FDE loop?
answers.a: Seven stages: embed, discover, frame, design, build, evaluate, and demo and hand over. On a real engagement you go round more than once, each time with a sharper problem and a better build. Every module in the program maps to part of this loop.

answers.q: How is an FDE different from a consultant or solutions engineer?
answers.a: Ask what each delivers and to whom. A consultant gives advice to one client, a solutions engineer shows a convincing fit mostly before a sale, and a product engineer builds a product for many clients. An FDE delivers a working, evaluated system to one client and stays until an owner runs it.

answers.q: Why do AI pilots stall before production?
answers.a: The model is rarely the main problem. Pilots stall on five gaps around it: data, integration, validation, ownership and adoption. An FDE closes these on purpose from the start, for example by getting real data access on day one and naming the owner before building.

answers.q: How should I use AI to learn without fooling myself?
answers.a: The rule is: the AI may explain and check, but you must produce. Write your answer or code first, then ask the AI to find the gaps. Verify anything you will act on against an official source. If you cannot explain it without the chat window open, you have not learned it yet.

answers.q: How should my pair partner and I work together?
answers.a: Use driver and navigator: the driver types or builds, the navigator watches, asks questions and thinks one step ahead. Swap every 25 to 30 minutes. When the domain person drives a technical task, the software person explains instead of taking the keyboard, and the other way round. If one person is always driving, the pair is not working.

answers.q: Why does the same question get a different answer?
answers.a: At each step the model produces likelihoods and samples one token from them. Temperature controls how adventurous that choice is. One different token early on changes everything after it. So test a prompt on many cases, and check exact answers with code where you can.

answers.q: Does the model learn from my conversations?
answers.a: No. During inference the model's parameters do not change. If it seems to remember earlier messages in a chat, that is because they are sent again as part of the prompt. It also has a training cutoff, so give it recent facts in the prompt.

answers.q: How do I estimate what an LLM feature will cost?
answers.a: Measure typical input and output tokens per call on real examples. Look up the current price per million input and output tokens. Multiply each count by its price, divide by one million and add them for the cost per call. Multiply by calls per day and working days per month, and add a margin for retries and growth.

answers.q: Why are long prompts slower and more expensive?
answers.a: You pay for every input token on every call, and the model must process all input before the first token appears. Output is slower per token because each one needs its own pass. Send only the relevant parts, ask for shorter output, use a smaller model for simple tasks, use prompt caching, and stream responses.

answers.q: What makes a good prompt?
answers.a: Five parts cover most needs: role, task, context, examples and output format. The model cannot ask you questions mid-call, so anything you leave out it will guess. Be specific, for example 'under 80 words' rather than 'keep it short', and separate instructions from data with simple tags.

answers.q: How do I reduce hallucinations?
answers.a: Ground the model: put the real source material in the prompt and tell it to answer only from that. Ask for citations so a person can check each claim, and allow it to say 'I do not know'. Let code do important arithmetic. Grounding reduces hallucination but does not remove it, so keep evaluation and human review.

answers.q: Should I use RAG, tools or an agent?
answers.a: Use the simplest pattern that solves the problem. Answers from documents: RAG. Answers needing live system data or exact maths: tools. Known fixed steps: a workflow set by your code. Open-ended tasks with steps you cannot predict: an agent, with limits and review.

answers.q: Where should a person review AI output?
answers.a: Decide by the cost of an error. Low harm and easy to undo: let it run and sample a few each week. Medium harm, such as a draft customer reply: a person reviews and sends. High harm or hard to undo, such as a payment or a decision about a person: a person decides and the AI only prepares information.

answers.q: What do HTTP status codes like 401, 404 and 500 mean?
answers.a: Learn the families. 2xx is success, 3xx means look elsewhere, 4xx means the request was wrong, and 5xx means the server failed. 401 is not authenticated, 403 is not allowed, 404 is not found, 429 is too many requests. A 4xx means check what you sent; a 5xx means the other side has a problem.

answers.q: Why does my maths on CSV data give strange results?
answers.a: Data read from a CSV file always arrives as text. '120' + '5' gives '1205', and 9 can look bigger than 10 when compared as text. Convert numbers with float() or int() before doing maths. This is the most common beginner bug in data scripts.

answers.q: How do I read a Python error message?
answers.a: Read the traceback from the bottom up. The last line names the error type; the lines above show the file and line. KeyError usually means a column name is spelled differently, FileNotFoundError means you ran from another folder, and ValueError often means a value like 'n/a' reached float(). Add print() lines before the failing line and change one thing at a time.

answers.q: How do I keep an API key safe?
answers.a: Treat a key like a password. Keep it in an environment variable or a .env file that is never committed, and read it in code with os.environ. Never paste it into chat tools, tickets or screenshots. Ask the client for a key with the least access the proof of concept needs.

answers.q: Why are my API totals wrong, and what are rate limits?
answers.a: Big lists are split into pages; if you forget to loop through them you silently process only the first page. Rate limits cap calls per period, and going over returns 429, often with a Retry-After header. Wait as the API asks and cap your retries. Always check the status code before using the body.

answers.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
answers.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters totals after GROUP BY. An ordinary JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides, so an invoice with an unknown supplier silently disappears. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first table and fills the gap with NULL, which makes problems visible.

answers.q: I committed a secret to Git. What do I do?
answers.a: Treat it as leaked: tell the owner, revoke the key and create a new one. Deleting the file is not enough because it stays in the history. Prevent it next time with a .gitignore that lists .env, and read git status before every commit.

answers.q: How do I review code an AI assistant wrote?
answers.a: Read every change as a diff. Check it does only what you asked, that you understand every line, and that you ran it and the tests passed. Check what happens with blank or wrong input, that every library and API field really exists, and that no secrets or customer data are in code or prompts. You own every line you hand over.

answers.q: What is a system of record?
answers.a: It is the one system the company treats as the official source of truth for a type of data, such as the ERP for invoices or the CRM for customers. If a spreadsheet disagrees, the system of record wins. Any automation that writes data must write there, or it creates a second truth someone has to reconcile by hand.

answers.q: Where do cost and delay hide in a business?
answers.a: At handoffs, where work moves between teams or systems. Look for four signs: the same data re-keyed into two systems, work waiting in a queue, rework after mistakes, and exceptions that go to a person. Exceptions are often a small share of volume but a large share of effort.

answers.q: What are the Business Model Canvas and Value Proposition Canvas for?
answers.a: The Business Model Canvas describes the whole company on one page in nine blocks. The Value Proposition Canvas zooms into one user group: their jobs, pains and gains, and how your offer relieves pains and creates gains. Treat them as structured note-taking, and make every entry trace to something someone said or you saw.

answers.q: What should a market scan include?
answers.a: List options in five groups: dedicated products, features in systems the client already owns, people-based options, general tools, and doing nothing. Do nothing is the real baseline your option must beat. Mark vendor claims as 'vendor says', score options on the client's criteria, and keep it to one page.

answers.q: How do I build a business case?
answers.a: Start with volume times time saved per case times loaded cost per hour. Add quality and risk effects only where you have a basis, then subtract build and run costs. Take volume from system data, time from timing real cases, and loaded cost from finance. Show a low, base and high case and the payback month.

answers.q: Are saved hours the same as cash savings?
answers.a: No. Hours saved only become cash if something changes, such as a vacancy not filled, a contractor released or overtime stopping. Otherwise they are capacity people spend on other work. Say clearly which it is, ask the sponsor what they would do with the hours, and never imply headcount cuts they have not discussed.

answers.q: Should we build, buy or configure?
answers.a: Ask in order. First, can a system the client already owns do it well enough with configuration? If not, does a mature product do it? Build only when the need is specific to the client's process and someone can own the result. Real solutions are often a mix, with a thin custom layer only where the client is different.

answers.q: How do I run a good discovery interview?
answers.a: Ask about the last real case: 'Walk me through the last invoice exception you handled.' Talk about their life, not your idea, ask about specifics in the past, not opinions about the future, and listen more than you talk. When someone says 'always' or 'usually', ask for the last time it happened. Do not pitch your solution during the interview.

answers.q: What is the difference between touch time and elapsed time?
answers.a: Touch time is how long someone actively works on a case. Elapsed time is from arrival to completion, including waiting. A case might take 12 minutes of touch time but five days elapsed waiting for approval. They lead to different solutions: one saves effort, the other removes waiting.

answers.q: What if interviews and system logs tell different stories?
answers.a: Disagreement is a finding, not a failure. People often describe touch time while logs show elapsed time, and logs show rework or skipped steps people do not mention. Take the difference back to the people involved without blame and ask if it matches what they see. Their explanation usually reveals the real rule or the real pain.

answers.q: How do I draw a process map?
answers.a: Build from your evidence. Agree the start and end, list the standard steps as verb plus object, put each in a lane for its role or system, add decisions as gateways, then add exceptions and label each step with its system and time. Draw the happy path first. Map the current state and get it agreed before drawing the future state.

answers.q: What is a RACI?
answers.a: A RACI lists tasks or decisions down the side and people across the top. R is Responsible (does the work), A is Accountable (owns and signs off), C is Consulted (input before), and I is Informed (told after). The key rule is exactly one A per row; if two people are accountable, nobody is.

answers.q: What goes in a one-page brief, and how do I write acceptance criteria for AI?
answers.a: The brief states the problem, who has it, today's baseline, success measures, what is in and out of scope, user stories, data, constraints, risks and owners. For AI, write criteria over a set of cases, such as 'matches the AP lead's judgement in at least 45 of 50 cases', plus what it does when unsure and what it must never do alone. Get explicit sign-off before you build; a short 'Agreed' email is enough.

answers.q: Why do people resist new tools, and what is ADKAR?
answers.a: Resistance is usually reasonable and tells you what is missing: fear for jobs, extra work, past failed tools, unclear benefit or not being asked. ADKAR breaks change into Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement; find the first stage someone has not reached and work on that. Bring the process owner along from week one.

answers.q: What are the three automation levels?
answers.a: Assistive: the AI suggests and a person decides and acts. Semi-automated: the AI does the work and a person approves or corrects before anything leaves. Automated: the AI acts alone and people look at samples and exceptions. A common path is to start semi-automated and move low-risk categories up once the correction rate is low and stable.

answers.q: Can I use the model's confidence score to decide what a person checks?
answers.a: Be careful. Language models do not produce a reliable built-in probability that an answer is right. Build your own signals instead: missing required fields, values that fail business rules, disagreement between two checks, or results from an evaluation on labelled examples.

answers.q: What is the C4 model?
answers.a: C4 draws architecture at four zoom levels: context, containers, components and code. For most FDE work the first two are enough. The context diagram shows your system, its users and the external systems it talks to, including the model API. The container diagram shows the separately running parts, with every arrow labelled with what flows and how.

answers.q: How does my solution get data in and out of client systems?
answers.a: There are four common patterns: API calls (pull), webhooks (push), batch files and event streams. For a POC, a file export is often the fastest route to realistic data. Start read-only; when you write back, write to a draft or review state first and make writes idempotent. Map every place data goes, including the model provider.

answers.q: What are the main security risks of an LLM app?
answers.a: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is a widely used checklist. The ones an FDE meets most are prompt injection, data leakage and secrets, excessive agency, and unbounded cost. Mark outside content as data, filter documents by user permission before they reach the model, keep tools narrow with approval for risky actions, keep secrets out of prompts, and keep an audit trail.

answers.q: How do I choose a model and estimate its monthly cost?
answers.a: Choose on criteria: quality on the client's own examples, latency, cost at expected volume, data rules and effort to operate. Monthly cost is requests per month times (input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price), divided by one million. Input includes the system prompt, retrieved text and tool definitions. Start with a capable model, then test a smaller one on the same evaluation set.

answers.q: Should I build in a low-code tool like n8n or write custom code?
answers.a: Decide by who will run and change it after you leave. Low-code fits simple trigger-and-action flows with existing connectors and a team that already maintains that tool. Custom code fits complex logic, an evaluation suite on every change, high volume or strict security. A hybrid is common, and either way keep prompts, schemas and eval sets in version control.

answers.q: How do I get reliable JSON from the model in code?
answers.a: Ask for JSON that follows a schema you define; structured outputs can constrain the response to that schema. Then validate in two steps: parse into a typed object, and apply business rules such as positive totals and allowed currencies. A schema guarantees shape, not truth. Never pass unchecked model output into a database or another system.

answers.q: What does finish_reason tell me?
answers.a: stop means the model finished normally. length means it ran out of room and the output may be cut off. content_filter means the provider blocked the answer. Check it on every call and handle each case on purpose.

answers.q: How does tool use work?
answers.a: You describe tools with a name, a description and an input schema. When the model wants one, it replies with a tool call; it does not run anything. Your code runs the function, sends a tool message with the matching tool_call_id, and calls the model again until the reply has no tool calls. The model proposes and your code disposes.

answers.q: What should a tool return when it fails?
answers.a: Still send a tool message, say clearly that the call failed and describe the problem in words, such as 'no order with that id'. The model can then ask the user instead of inventing an answer. Also validate the input before running anything, including whether the current user may see that data.

answers.q: Should RAG use keyword search or embeddings?
answers.a: Keyword search is simple, fast and great for exact terms like product codes. Embedding search matches meaning, so 'annual leave' can find 'vacation days', but needs an embedding model and vector storage. Many production systems use both. For a first POC, keyword search is often good enough and much easier to debug.

answers.q: My RAG answers are wrong. Where do I look first?
answers.a: Look at what was retrieved first. Most RAG problems are retrieval problems: the right chunk was never found, was split in half, or was ranked below irrelevant ones. Test retrieval and generation separately, with 20 to 50 real questions and the chunk that should answer each.

answers.q: When should I build an agent instead of a workflow?
answers.a: If you can draw the steps in advance, build a workflow; it is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Use an agent only when the steps truly depend on what is found along the way, with a clear finish line. Put guardrails in code: a turn and cost limit, few read-only tools, approval for risky actions, an audit log and a hand-over to a person when stuck.

answers.q: When is building an MCP server worth it?
answers.a: When the same capability will be used from more than one host, when staff want company data inside off-the-shelf assistants, or when a ready-made server already exists. For one app with two or three tools, plain tool use is simpler. Test a server with the MCP Inspector before connecting it, and in a stdio server log to standard error, not standard output.

answers.q: How do I decide which steps need code, a model or a person?
answers.a: Take each step in turn. If you can write the rule as if/else, a lookup or an API call, it is code. If it needs reading or writing messy human language, a model handles it. If a wrong answer costs money, breaks a law or is hard to undo, a person approves it. Often only a few steps need a model.

answers.q: How do I design for things going wrong?
answers.a: Build a failure modes catalogue: each failure, how you detect it and what the system does. Treat every model output as untrusted: validate its shape, then its meaning with business rules. Retry only temporary errors, and route invalid or low-confidence cases to a person with the reason attached.

answers.q: What is idempotency and why does it matter for retries?
answers.a: Idempotent means doing a write twice has the same effect as doing it once. Retries repeat work, so without it a timeout after a successful write can post the same invoice twice. Give each item a stable key and check it before writing. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and stop after a fixed number of tries.

answers.q: How do I approach a vague ask like 'use AI in our factory'?
answers.a: Work in order and think out loud. Clarify the ask, find the real bottleneck, agree one success measure, then propose the smallest MVP that proves value with a person in control. Only then describe the production design: model, harness, tools and permissions, context, evals, observability, cost, security and deployment.

answers.q: How do I roll out an AI solution safely?
answers.a: Build on top of the client's systems, not instead of them. Then move up a ladder: test environment, shadow mode where the AI writes nothing, assisted mode with approval, more autonomy for clearly low-risk cases, then production. Move up only with agreed evidence, and keep a feature toggle to switch the AI step off quickly.

answers.q: What makes a strong portfolio project?
answers.a: One deep project on one real bottleneck in an industry you care about, not a general chatbot. Use messy public data plus synthetic data, connect real infrastructure, handle edge cases with a review path, add a golden set with a pass rate, and deploy it. Write it up with scope, trade-offs, what broke and how you would run it for ten customers.

answers.q: What do FDE interviews look like?
answers.a: Loops differ, but candidates report a behavioral round, a technical deep dive with coding and system design, and a case study where you scope a vague problem aloud, sometimes with a take-home. Expect deep questions on your own project. Practise class design and live Python without an IDE, not only algorithm puzzles.

answers.q: What is an evaluation set?
answers.a: A list of example inputs, each with the output a competent person would expect. You run the solution on every input and count how often it is right, like a unit test. The value comes from real cases: invented ones are too clean. Store it as a plain file in the repository and rerun it after every prompt or model change.

answers.q: Who should label the expected answers?
answers.a: The people who own the work, not you. Sit with the subject matter expert, go through cases and record the reason next to each label. When two experts disagree, that is a finding: the client needs to decide a rule before any AI can follow it.

answers.q: How many cases does my eval set need?
answers.a: There is no magic size. Start with a few dozen cases that cover every case type, which you can label in an afternoon with an expert; the capstone minimum is 30. Grow it with every bug you find. Keep a held-back group you never look at while tuning, for an honest final check.

answers.q: How do I measure quality and find what to fix?
answers.a: Pick the simplest metric that fits, such as pass rate, and split it by case type. Then open every failed case, write one note on what went wrong, group the notes into causes and fix the biggest cause first. Change one thing between runs and keep a results file per run.

answers.q: Can I use an LLM to grade written answers such as summaries?
answers.a: Yes, an LLM-as-judge reads the input, the output and a list of narrow yes or no rules and returns pass or fail with a reason. Judges can be inconsistent and may prefer longer answers. Have the expert grade 20 or 30 outputs by hand, run the judge on the same ones, and only trust it where it agrees with the human.

answers.q: Where should a person approve, and what should I log?
answers.a: Always review actions that move money, change a customer record, send something out or affect a person's rights. Review when unsure for flagged cases, sample low-risk output, and skip review for internal drafts. Log a case id, the input, the output as shown, the model and prompt version, the reviewer, their decision and reason, and timestamps.

answers.q: Should I deploy as a static page, serverless or a container?
answers.a: A static page is simplest but cannot hold secrets. Serverless runs code on demand and can hold the API key on the server side, with limits on run time. Containers give the most control and suit long-running work or clients who want everything in their own cloud. A common POC shape is a static front end plus one serverless or container API.

answers.q: How do I handle secrets and stop a prompt change from breaking quality?
answers.a: Keep secrets outside code: environment variables locally, repository secrets in CI, and the cloud's secret store in production, with a different key per environment. Add an eval gate to CI that fails if the pass rate drops below an agreed threshold. Keep prompts in Git so they go through the same review and can be rolled back.

answers.q: How should I structure a demo?
answers.a: Tell a short story: the problem in the client's words, the result on their real cases, evidence from the eval set, the honest limits, and a clear ask. Before building any slide, write down the one decision you want at the end. Use the client's words, not your jargon.

answers.q: Should I show a failure in my demo?
answers.a: Yes. Show at least one case where the solution is wrong or refuses, and how the workflow catches it; it builds more trust than a perfect run. Rehearse twice and keep a recorded run as a backup. If something breaks, switch to the recording calmly.

answers.q: What is the difference between a POC, a pilot and production?
answers.a: A POC answers 'can this work at all on our cases?'. A pilot answers 'does it work for real users in daily work, and is it worth it?'. Production answers 'can the business rely on it every day, at full volume, safely?'. Each needs more engineering, and ownership shifts from the FDE to the client as you move up.

answers.q: Is it a failure if the client decides to stop after a POC?
answers.a: No, stopping is a valid result. A POC that shows the data is too poor, or a pilot that shows the time saved is too small, saves the client from a larger failed project. Agree exit criteria in writing before each stage, then recommend move on, another round, or stop.

answers.q: How do I prioritise what to build next?
answers.a: Plan around outcomes, changes in the business, not outputs you build. Score each backlog item on value and effort with the client: do high value, low effort first; break up high value, high effort; park low value, high effort and say why. Measure a baseline before you change anything.

answers.q: What goes in a hand-over pack?
answers.a: Three core parts: a runbook for daily operation and fixing problems, a named owner for the outcome and a team for the running system, and a support model saying who answers what and how fast. Start it on day one of the pilot. Before you leave, make sure the client owns every account and key, and run a shadow period.

answers.q: How does the final project work?
answers.a: You and your partner pick one use case and a mentor plays the client. Week 11 is about the problem: discovery, a process map, the one-page brief, an options paper and the start of the evaluation set. Week 12 is build, evaluate, deploy behind access control, and a ten-minute demo to the panel on day 10.

answers.q: What are the rules of the capstone?
answers.a: Use only the data the mock client gives you, or synthetic data labelled as synthetic. Never paste real personal data into a public tool. Every claim in the brief, options paper and demo must point to evidence. If you change scope, write it down and get the client to agree.

answers.q: What goes in the options paper?
answers.a: Two to three pages describing two or three genuinely different options, compared on the same rows: effect on the success measure, accuracy risk, cost, time to build, security and privacy, and effort to adopt. Include a non-AI option when one is plausible. End with a recommendation, what would change your mind, and the next step.

answers.q: What goes in the evaluation sheet?
answers.a: One row per case with case_id, input, expected, type (normal, edge or out_of_scope), output, pass and a failure_note for every no. Take most cases at random from the client's sample, add edge cases from discovery and a few out-of-scope ones. Thirty cases is the minimum, enough to find the main failure types but not a precise accuracy figure.

answers.q: How is the ten-minute capstone demo laid out?
answers.a: Minute 0 to 1 is the problem and baseline, 1 to 2 the process map with the changed step, and 2 to 6 a live run on one normal and one hard case. Minute 6 to 8 is the evaluation result and top failures, 8 to 9 the limits and risks, and 9 to 10 the next step, its cost and who must say yes. Each partner presents part and answers questions on any part.

answers.q: Can I use an LLM to help write my brief?
answers.a: Yes, for turning interview notes into a draft, finding gaps, or playing a skeptical sponsor. It is not a source of facts about the client. Every number and claim must come from your notes, documents or data. Ask it to mark each sentence with the note it came from, and delete any sentence it cannot source.
